label: Date
why: The date is the first token in every filename this tool renders, and sorts your files chronologically without you having to name them that way.

prompt: What kind of experiment is this?
label: Experiment type
why: A short code that groups related acquisitions together in a folder listing -- for example CT for a control, G1G2 for a two-generation comparison. Make up your own short code if these don't fit.

prompt: What is the sample or specimen identifier?
label: Sample ID
why: A short code unique to this specimen -- a three-letter code plus two digits, like ABC01 or XYZ12. It is what tells two files apart when they share the same date and experiment type.

prompt: What magnification is this acquired at?
label: Magnification
why: The zoom level or objective, like 40x or 100x -- lets you filter your files later (e.g. finding every 63x acquisition).

prompt: Which markers or fluorophores are you imaging?
label: Markers
why: The stains, dyes, or fluorescent proteins you are imaging, like DAPI or GFP -- the main thing collaborators search filenames for.

prompt: What organism or cell line is this?
label: Organism / cell line
why: Groups this experiment with others on the same model system when you're searching later.

prompt: What type of sample is this?
label: Sample type
placeholder: e.g. tissue section, cell culture, whole mount
why: Sample type changes what acquisition settings and controls are typical -- later steps use this to tailor their suggestions.

label: Preparation
placeholder: e.g. fixed in 4% PFA, frozen section
why: Fixation and mounting method affects which controls and settings make sense, and is easy to forget by the time you write the paper.

label: Instrument
why: Ties this experiment to the instrument's known objectives, lasers, and detectors for later acquisition guidance.

label: Modality
why: Confocal, widefield, and STED each have different pitfalls worth flagging here. Not every modality is optical: SEM/TEM/Raman samples typically have no biological or technical replicates in the usual sense, which is why those are separate, independently-optional questions.

prompt: What is the smallest feature you need to resolve?
label: Smallest feature (nm)
why: This is the number that actually sets how finely to sample the image (Nyquist sampling) -- worth deciding before you're at the microscope, not after. Leave blank if you haven't decided.

label: Readout
why: What you are actually measuring -- a viability assay, a ROS assay, and a migration assay each need a different reference control, and the app can only suggest the right ones once it knows which you're running.

prompt: Anything else worth noting about this acquisition?
label: Notes
why: A free-text escape hatch for anything the other questions didn't capture -- entirely optional.

prompt: How long does fixation and staining take?
label: Fixation & staining
why: From start to a sample ready for the scope. Bench-prep time is usually the first bottleneck in a session -- knowing it lets the schedule (and the .ics export) block out a realistic slot instead of assuming zero.

prompt: How long does mounting take, per sample?
label: Mounting (per sample)
why: Mounting time scales with your sample count, so this is multiplied by however many samples the design plans -- worth a real estimate, not a guess made once at the scope.

prompt: How long does one acquisition take at the microscope, per sample?
label: Acquisition (per sample)
why: This is usually the largest block on the schedule and the one most worth booking shared-instrument time around.

prompt: How long do you expect image analysis and processing to take, in total?
label: Image analysis (total)
why: Analysis time is easy to leave off a schedule entirely -- a rough estimate here is enough to stop the project from looking 'done' the moment acquisition finishes.
